Debrecen
DEB-ret-sen
n. (the Hungarian market town on the great plain called the Calvinist Rome, seat of the confession of 1562 and the synod of 1567)
Hungarian Debrecen, perhaps from a Slavic or Turkic personal name; the town is first named in 1235.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Debrecen is the town that gave the Hungarian Reformed church its confession, its press and its college, and it did so under Ottoman overlordship with no prince to protect it. A cattle-market town on the treeless plain, it had no walls, no bishop and no university, and it turned Reformed in the 1550s under Martin Kalmancsehi and then Peter Melius, who was its minister from 1558 and the organiser of the Hungarian church. The Debrecen Confession of 1562, drawn up by Melius and Gergely Szegedi, set out the Reformed faith against both Rome and the antitrinitarians in Hungarian. The Synod of Debrecen in 1567 adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, settled a presbyterian-synodical order, and fixed the doctrine of the Magyar church for four centuries. The town's press printed in Hungarian from 1561, its college trained the ministry and sent its best students to Wittenberg, Heidelberg, Franeker and Leiden, and Gyorgy Martonfalvi taught there against the Jesuits. It is called the Calvinist Rome because for three hundred years every Hungarian Reformed minister passed through it. The dictionary enters Debrecen because it shows a church fully furnished with the three things that outlast persecution: a confession, a press and a school.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer; a college as a society of men for the pursuit of learning; and a press as the business of printing.

expand to see more

SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of ministers and elders.

CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

COLLEGE, n. A society of men invested with certain powers, engaged in some common pursuit, chiefly of learning.

PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing.

MARKET, n. A public place in a city or town where provisions or cattle are exposed for sale; the rate of purchase and sale.

Key Scripture

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

2Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Act 16:5 — "And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily."

Modern Corruption

Hungarian market town on the plain, Reformed from the 1550s, which produced the Confession of 1562 and the Synod of 1567 and trained the Magyar ministry.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the revival that leaves nothing behind, and Debrecen is the reproof of it. Hungary in the 1550s was full of preaching and short of order; what Melius added was a confession in the vernacular, a printed catechism, a synod that could meet and decide, and a college that examined the men it sent out. None of that is glamorous and all of it is what survived the Jesuits, the Habsburg commissions and the Decade of Mourning. “And when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) is the apostolic pattern, and the pattern is unexciting on purpose.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is teaching that aims at understanding rather than at impression. “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) is the whole programme of the Debrecen press and the Debrecen college, and a minister trained there was expected to be “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15). The result is what is recorded of the churches of Asia, that “so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily” (Act 16:5).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bin (H995), to discern, to understand; Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint by vote.

expand to see more

Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, to consider, to cause to understand; “caused them to understand the reading”, Nehemiah 8:8.

Hebrew parash (H6567) — to make distinct, to declare plainly; “they read in the book in the law of God distinctly”, Nehemiah 8:8.

Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to handle rightly; “rightly dividing the word of truth”, 2 Timothy 2:15.

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, to designate by a show of hands; “when they had ordained them elders in every church”, Acts 14:23.

Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, to make firm; “were the churches established in the faith”, Acts 16:5.

Usage

"“caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — the Hungarian press at Debrecen from 1561."

"“a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15) — the college that examined the Magyar ministry."

"“were the churches established in the faith” (Act 16:5) — the Synod of 1567 adopting the Second Helvetic Confession."
